_comment: Readiness quiz bank (ID document, appendix B). One item per slot is shown; variant A first, an unseen variant on retry. Every wrong option names the misconception (M1-M5, ID section 3.4) it targets. Rules are applied by js/quiz/quiz-engine.js. Any change must be checked against the Java DFS output (ticket C-02).

items.prompt: What does DFS use to remember which nodes it still has to explore?

options.text: Stack
options.feedback: Correct. DFS always continues from the node it saw most recently, and a stack gives back the most recent item first.

options.text: Queue
options.feedback: Not quite. A queue gives back the *oldest* item first, which explores the tree level by level. That is breadth-first search. DFS needs the newest item first: a stack.

options.text: Sorted list
options.feedback: Not quite. DFS does not use the order of the values at all. It needs to remember *where to go back to*, which a stack does.

options.text: Nothing; it just follows the lines
options.feedback: Not quite. After a leaf, DFS has to know where to go back to. Something must remember that: a stack.

items.prompt: You insert 65 into tree A. Where does it go?

options.text: Right child of 60
options.feedback: Correct. 65 > 50: go right. 65 < 70: go left to 60. 65 > 60: go right, which is empty, so 65 goes there.

options.text: Left child of 70
options.feedback: Close, but 70 already has a left child (60). Keep comparing until you reach an empty spot.

options.text: Right child of 80
options.feedback: Not quite. 65 is smaller than 70, so at 70 you go left, not right.

options.text: Left child of 60
options.feedback: Not quite. 65 is larger than 60, so it goes to the right of 60.

items.prompt: DFS (pre-order) has just visited 30 in tree A. Which node does it visit next?

options.feedback: Correct. DFS goes as deep as possible first, starting with the left child.
Not quite. 70 is on the same level as 30, so that would be moving across. Depth-first goes down first.
Not quite. 40 is 30's right child. DFS pushes right first, then left, so the left child 20 is on top and comes off first.
Not quite. DFS only goes back up (backtracks) when it reaches a leaf. 30 still has children to explore.

items.prompt: Which sentence best describes backtracking in DFS?

options.text: Going back to the most recent node that still has an unexplored child
options.feedback: Correct. That is exactly what popping the next node off the stack achieves.

options.text: Starting again from the root
options.feedback: Not quite. DFS never restarts. It continues from the most recent point that still has something left to explore.

options.text: Visiting the nodes in reverse order
options.feedback: Not quite. Backtracking is about where to go *next* after a dead end, not about reversing the order.

options.text: Moving to the next node on the same level
options.feedback: Not quite. That describes breadth-first search. In DFS, backtracking goes back *up* to a node you have already passed.

items.prompt: Put the nodes of tree A in pre-order.
items.correctFeedback: Correct. Each node is written down when you first arrive, before its children.

rules.feedback: That is in-order. In pre-order a node comes *before* its children, so the root 50 comes first.
That is post-order. In pre-order the root comes first, not last.
That is level by level (breadth-first). Pre-order finishes the whole left subtree before moving to 70.

items.fallbackFeedback: Not quite. Position {position} should be {expected}. Walk the tree again: write each node down when you first arrive, then go left before right.

items.prompt: Put the nodes of tree B in in-order.
items.correctFeedback: Correct, and sorted, as in-order of a BST always is.

rules.feedback: That is pre-order. In in-order you write a node down *between* its left and right subtrees.
Very close. Look at 35 and 30: 30 is 35's left child, so it must come before 35.
That is post-order. Hint: for a BST, the in-order is always sorted.

items.fallbackFeedback: Not quite. Position {position} should be {expected}. Hint: for a BST, the in-order is always sorted.

items.prompt: During a DFS search on tree A the stack is [40, 70], top first. Which node is popped next?

options.feedback: Correct. The top of the stack is written first. 40 was pushed after 70, so it comes off first.
Not quite. 70 is at the bottom. A stack gives back the last item pushed, which is 40.
Not quite. 20 is no longer on the stack; it has already been visited.
Not quite. The root was the first node visited and is no longer on the stack.

items.prompt: DFS is searching tree A for 60 and has just visited 70. What is on the stack now (top first)?

options.feedback: Correct. 80 (right) was pushed first, then 60 (left), so 60 is on top.
Not quite. Right is pushed first and left last, so the left child 60 ends up on top.
Not quite. 70 has just been visited, so it has already been popped off.
Not quite. Both children of 70 are pushed, not just the one we are looking for. DFS does not know where 60 is yet.

items.prompt: How many nodes does DFS visit to find 80 in tree A?

options.feedback: Correct. DFS explores the whole left subtree (30, 20, 40) and then 70 and 60 before reaching 80. 80 is the last node visited.
That would be right if DFS used the BST rule (50, 70, 80). Plain DFS does not look at values, so it explores the left side first.
Not quite. DFS always starts at the root and checks every node it passes on the way.

items.prompt: How many nodes does DFS visit to find 30 in tree B?

options.feedback: That is the BST-rule path (45, 25, 35, 30). DFS also visits 15, because it always goes left first.
Not quite. DFS stops as soon as it finds the target. It never reaches the right subtree.
Not quite. Count each node DFS visits, starting from the root: 45, 25, 15, 35, 30.

items.prompt: Why is the in-order of a BST always sorted?

options.text: Everything left of a node is smaller and everything right is larger, and in-order writes left, then the node, then right
options.feedback: Correct. That holds at every node, so the whole list comes out from smallest to largest.

options.text: Because DFS compares values as it goes
options.feedback: Not quite. DFS never compares values to decide where to go. The sorting comes from the shape of the BST.

options.text: It only happens for this particular tree
options.feedback: Not quite. Try building your own BST in the sandbox: in-order is sorted every time.

options.text: Because inserting a value sorts the tree
options.feedback: Not quite. Inserting places a value in the right position, but the tree itself is not a sorted list. In-order is what reads it out in order.

items.prompt: A classmate says: "On a BST, DFS goes right whenever the target is bigger." What is wrong?

options.text: DFS ignores the values and always goes left first; the classmate is describing a different search
options.feedback: Correct. That rule describes BST search, which you will meet in the lecture. Plain DFS explores blindly, left first.

options.text: Nothing, it is correct
options.feedback: Not quite. That is a common mix-up. DFS does not use the ordering; it always goes left first.

options.text: DFS goes left when the target is bigger
options.feedback: Not quite. DFS does not compare the target to choose a direction at all.

options.text: DFS chooses a direction at random
options.feedback: Not quite. DFS is completely predictable: always left first, then right.
